summary: Psalm 100 calls all lands to joyful worship of Yahweh. It moves from shouted praise and glad service to a confession that Yahweh is God, maker, owner, shepherd, and faithful one. The psalm ends by grounding thanksgiving in Yahweh's goodness, loving kindness, and faithfulness.
whyItMatters: This short psalm gives a compact picture of praise in Book IV of Psalms: worship is public, joyful, and based on who Yahweh is. It also shows how thanksgiving and praise are joined to the claim that God's care reaches “all generations.”

context.author: Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections; this psalm's heading names it “A Psalm of thanksgiving,” but the heading does not identify a named author.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that adopted the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to all the Psalms would be misleading.
context.setting: The psalm imagines worshipers approaching Yahweh's gates and courts, language oriented toward public worship.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, here a brief thanksgiving psalm built from commands to praise and reasons for praise.

outline.heading: A worldwide summons
outline.note: The psalm opens with the heading and a call for all lands to shout joyfully to Yahweh.

outline.heading: Glad service and singing
outline.note: The worshipers are told to serve Yahweh with gladness and come before him with singing.

outline.heading: Knowing who Yahweh is
outline.note: The psalm identifies Yahweh as God, maker, owner, and shepherd of his people.

outline.heading: Entering with thanks
outline.note: The worshipers are invited into gates and courts with thanksgiving, praise, thanks, and blessing.

outline.heading: The reason for praise
outline.note: The closing verse explains the summons: Yahweh is good, and his loving kindness and faithfulness endure.

keyVerses.text: A Psalm of thanksgiving. Shout for joy to Yahweh, all you lands!
keyVerses.why: This opening names the psalm as thanksgiving and immediately widens the summons beyond one local group.

keyVerses.text: Know that Yahweh, he is God. It is he who has made us, and we are his. We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the central confession behind the chapter's worship: Yahweh is God, maker, and shepherd.

keyVerses.text: Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise. Give thanks to him, and bless his name.
keyVerses.why: This verse pictures worship as an approach marked by gratitude, praise, and blessing.

keyVerses.text: For Yahweh is good. His loving kindness endures forever, his faithfulness to all generations.
keyVerses.why: The final verse states the reason the commands make sense: Yahweh's goodness, loving kindness, and faithfulness last.

questions.question: What kind of psalm is this?
questions.answer: The first words call it “A Psalm of thanksgiving.” The chapter fits that label because it repeatedly tells worshipers to shout, serve, come, enter, give thanks, and bless Yahweh. Its gratitude is based on who Yahweh is and what endures about him.

questions.question: Who is being called to praise?
questions.answer: Verse 1 addresses “all you lands,” so the summons is wider than one small group standing in one place. The psalm also speaks of “us” and “his people” in verse 3, so it includes a worshiping community that understands itself as belonging to Yahweh.

questions.question: What does “Serve Yahweh with gladness” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: In this psalm, serving Yahweh is not described as grim obligation. Verse 2 joins service with gladness and singing, and verse 4 joins approach to worship with thanksgiving and praise. The chapter presents worshipful service as joyful response to Yahweh.

questions.question: Why does verse 3 say “Know that Yahweh, he is God”?
questions.answer: The command to know gives the reason for the worship that surrounds it. The verse says Yahweh is God, that he made “us,” and that “we are his.” The psalm's praise is therefore grounded in belonging to the one it names as God.

questions.question: What is meant by “the sheep of his pasture”?
questions.answer: The phrase pictures Yahweh's people as a flock under his care. The verse does not develop the image at length, but it places “his people” and “the sheep of his pasture” side by side. The point in this chapter is belonging and care, not an extended farming description.

questions.question: Are the “gates” and “courts” literal places?
questions.answer: Verse 4 uses language of entering gates and courts, which fits public worship oriented toward a sacred place. Many psalms are oriented toward Jerusalem and its temple, though this chapter itself does not name Jerusalem. Readers should notice the worship setting without adding details the psalm does not give.

questions.question: Why does the psalm command joy and thanksgiving? Can feelings be commanded?
questions.answer: The psalm does use commands: shout, serve, come, enter, give thanks, and bless. It does not pause to analyze private emotion, but gives the worshiping community words and actions to perform before Yahweh. Readers differ on how directly this maps onto inner feeling, but the chapter itself connects the commands to Yahweh's goodness and faithfulness.

questions.question: What does the last verse add to the rest of the psalm?
questions.answer: Verse 5 explains why the praise is fitting. Yahweh is called good, his loving kindness is said to endure forever, and his faithfulness reaches all generations. The psalm ends with the character of Yahweh, not with the worshipers' performance.

glossary.def: Grateful acknowledgment directed to Yahweh; in this psalm it appears in the heading and again as part of entering his gates.
The divine name used throughout the hosted translation of this psalm.
A phrase in verse 5 describing Yahweh's enduring goodness toward his people.
A quality of Yahweh named in verse 5 and said to extend “to all generations.”
